ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
RCW 82.04.080 authorizes the imposition of a Business and Occupation tax (B& O tax)
on gross income rather than net income. Hence, as a general rule, the base amount from which
the B& O tax is calculated does not allow for deductions for the expenses of conducting business.
Even though business expenses are generally not deductible, the Department ofRevenue has
adopted WAC 458-20- 111 ( Rule 111); Rule 111 recognizes that certain "pass through" expenses
should not be included in determining gross income. The Hospitals base their arguments under
the following three WAC provisions: 458-20- 111 ( Rule 111); 458-20- 159 ( Rule 159); and 458-
20- 199 ( Rule 199).
Rule 159. The Board' s analysis will not focus on Rule 159. The Department argues it is
for tangible properties. The Board agrees. Even a quick reading of the regulation supports this
conclusion. The Hospitals argue the Board should apply it by analogy, admitting the literal
language ofRule 159 speaks only about tangible properties. The Board declines to interpret the
rule by analogy when it is limited by its literal language to tangible properties.
Rule 199. The Board' s analysis will not focus on Rule 199. The Department argues the

Rule 111. This Rule controls the outcome ofthese cases in the Board ofTax Appeals
opinion. Rule 111 is stated as follows:
WAC 458-20-111 Advances and reimbursements.
The word "advance" as used herein, means money or credits received by a taxpayer from
a customer or client with which the taxpayer is to pay costs or fees for the customer or
client.

The word " reimbursement" as used herein, means money or credits received from a
customer or client to repay the taxpayer for money or credits expended by the taxpayer in
payment of cost or fees for the client.
The words " advance" or "reimbursement" apply only when the customer or client alone is
liable for the payment of the fees or costs and when the taxpayer making the payment has no
personal liability therefor, either primarily or secondarily, other than as agent for the
customer or client.
There may be excluded from the measure of tax amounts representing money or credit
received by a taxpayer as reimbursement of an advance in accordance with the regular and
usual custom ofhis business or profession.
The foregoing is limited to cases wherein the taxpayer, as an incident to the business,
undertakes, on behalf of the customer, guest or client, the payment ofmoney, either upon an
obligation owing by the customer, guest or client to a third person, or in procuring a service
for the customer, guest or client which the does not or cannot render and for which no
liability attaches to the taxpayer. It does not apply to cases where the customer, guest or
client makes advances to the taxpayer upon services to be rendered by the taxpayer or upon
goods to be purchased by the taxpayer in carrying on the business in which the taxpayer
engages.
For example, where a taxpayer engaging in the business of selling automobiles at retail
collects from a customer, in addition to the purchase price, an amount sufficient to pay the
fees for automobile license, tax and registration of title, the amount so collected is not
properly a part of the gross sales ofthe taxpayer but is merely an advance and should be
excluded from gross proceeds of sales. Likewise, where an attorney pays filing fees or court
costs in any litigation, such fees and costs are paid as agent for the client and should be
excluded from the gross income of the attorney.
On the other hand, no charge which represents an advance payment on the purchase price
of an article or a cost of doing or obtaining business, even though such charge is made as a
separate item, will be construed as an advance or reimbursement. Money so received
constitutes a part of gross sales or gross income ofthe business, as the case may be. For
example, no exclusion is allowed with respect to amounts received by (1) a doctor for
furnishing medicine or drugs as a part ofhis treatment; (2) a dentist for furnishing gold,
silver or other property in conjunction with his services; ( 3) a garage for furnishing parts in

The first issue is the payment ofthe fee for the collection services provided. This is a
contractual requirement for all three hospitals. The hospitals have a right to retain a certain
percentage of monies collected to pay the prescribed fee. In some instances, the hospitals chose
not to be paid their full fees. Non-payment or underpayment does not alter the fact that the fees
are payable.
The second issue is the provision for uncollectible amounts. As prudent businesses, the
hospitals do not want to remit more than they have collected. They have therefore provided for a
means to determine uncollected or uncollectible amounts. There is no requirement that this
determination must be made on an invoice -by -invoice basis; there is no indication of any
preferred method for calculation ofuncollected amounts. Because ofthe sheer volume of
emergency room transactions, the individual charges become a fungible part of the whole.
Black' s Law Dictionary defines " fungible" as " regarded as commercially interchangeable with
other property of the same kind." 19 Just as it would be unreasonable to sort through a store of
apples to find the bad one, so is it unreasonable to expect the hospitals to track tens of thousands
of emergency room invoices individually. The hospitals, ESN, EPS, and the doctors (in the case
of Sacred Heart) have agreed to a methodology they find adequate to account for uncollectible
amounts.
The first prong of the Rule 111 test20 states the reimbursement of an advance may be
excluded if it is a part of the regular and usual custom of the business or profession. In the
timeline ofpayment for emergency room services, we know that a minority ofpatients pay cash
at the time of service. Some percentage ofpatients have insurance coverage, and those payments
come in after delay for processing claims. The balance ofthe charges incurred do not involve
third party reimbursement, and the hospitals are dependent on the ability and good will ofthe
patients for payment. In short, we know it is the usual custom ofthe hospital business to wait for
payment.
We also know it is the usual custom for suppliers to want payment. None ofus can
purchase goods or services, saying, " I' ll pay you when I get paid." We know we may have thirty
days, but we have to pay in a relatively timely fashion or we lose our ability to purchase. The
hospital has many employees who are paid semi-monthly or monthly regardless of collections.
The hospitals pay timely for laundry, supplies, and numerous other costs of doing business. We
stretch the bounds ofcommon sense ifwe contend the payment methodology by the hospitals
with regard to the subject contracts should be different.
The two service companies ( ESN and EPS) and the individual doctors at Sacred Heart
have entered into contracts with the hospitals that they will provide services to the hospital and
the hospital will provide collection services to them. The terms of the collection services are that
the hospitals will be paid for their services; that the hospitals will not be responsible for paying

The reimbursements made by the hospitals may be excluded if they are a part of the
regular and usual custom ofthe business. The first prong of the test is met. The assumptions of
the patients and whether there is an implied agency relationship do not defeat the simple
language ofRule 111.
The third prong ofRule 111 is that the taxpayer (the hospitals) is not liable for the
payment. The contracts between the parties are clear on this point: There will be a reduction in
remittances from the hospitals to reflect the accounts they couldn' t collect. The hospitals have
assumed no liability and that is all that Rule 111 asks.
A great deal of discussion is devoted to what the patients assume. Do patients assume
that the doctors are employed by the hospitals? Do patients assume the hospitals are responsible
for paying doctors under some form of contract? Do patients assume the doctor will personally
send them bills? The patients may wonder how they will pay the bill, but I suspect they don' t
give much thought to whose name is on the top. These questions do not bear on the matter before
the Board.
There is also much made of the fact that the hospitals sometimes " overpaid" ESN, EPS,
or the doctors (in the case of Sacred Heart) by failing to withhold sufficient funds to cover their
contractual collection fees. This is akin to a car dealership selling cars at cost or at a loss to
DARE programs or school drivers' education classes. There are many reasons a business may
not charge its " going rate" for their service or product. In may be inadvertent; it may be for
advertising; it may be for charity. It does not alter the question before us. Are the hospitals
liable to pay ESN, EPS, or the doctors (in the case of Sacred Heart) for amounts they cannot
collect on their behalf? The contracts say the hospitals are not so liable. The third prong ofRule
111 is met.
